text:
looks like we are going to continue to need masks for a while. this review is for a box of 50 disposable masks.

they come packaged into 5 plastic bags of 10 masks in each box, so easy to pull out 10 to stick in your car or near the door of your house to grab when you leave. they are the ear model, so two bands that go behind your ear, folds to make it larger to cover your face, and a wire in the nose. i usually use a cloth mask, but have heard that these disposable, especially with a cloth mask over to hold it tightly to your face, provide a good amount of protection. when i know i will be in contact with someone who is infected, i will use a full n-95, but for trips to the store, these are perfect.

so far the first 10 are fine. none of the straps came loose, they all folded our right, they didn't break when putting them on or taking them off. many of the early masks, as companies were getting into producing them, seemed to have issues with the loops coming loose or not opening as they should. these do not seem to have any issues like those, appear to be good quality and a fair price.

text:
the extech ex655 clamp meter is a solid feeling mid-priced unit that adds several features over a basic multimeter: current measurement of ac or dc currents via the clamp (which must clamp just a single wire), non-contact ac voltage detector, min/max capability, and a temperature probe.

i found the display challenging to read in all but very bright conditions because it is inset within the device so deeply as to be shadowed by the case. pressing the light button was hit or miss if the internal light would illuminate the display and even when that did work, the light went out too soon for me to complete my measurements without having to press it again. it is convenient to have a light to illuminate the clamps if you're working in low-light conditions while aiming for a wire. but, the button is located right where my thumb would be gripping the meter to open the clamp, making it uncomfortable not pressing the button in normal conditions. it also seems weird to me that the clamp light does not also automatically cause the display light to illuminate, as i'd think if you can't see the wire you're clamping, you won't be able to see the display either... so the display light requires a separate/awkward press-and-hold.

the temperature probe was quite inaccurate for temps below zero f, reading -1 when it should have read -15. checking dc amperage on either negative or positive cables in my car resulted in wildly swinging numbers. i've never had a clamp meter before, so don't know if that it so be expected (vs some reasonable measurement) or if the idea is just to confirm that current is slowing.

overall, for my capability to judge, the meter seems fine, but not as readable and usable for measurements where you'd use the test leads as extech's standard multimeters which have a better display and a kick-stand to hold the meter up at a decent viewing angle. if you don't need the clamp meter functionality, get a standard multimeter and a separate, inexpensive, non-contact ac voltage detector.

we could probably have used one the cheaper "pocket" wire checkers that most people use when swapping out light fixtures, but with this, we don't have to have exposed wire to know if there is current passing through the cable/wire or not.
i know this is used in more highly specialized applications, but we think it's very handy thing to have in a home renovator's toolbox!
